sections: Identify an exponential model's starting value
Find f(0) from an equation, graph, table, or context, including shifted and vertically translated models.
The start is the output at zero
An initial value is f(0). For the standard exponential f(x)=a·b^x, the initial value is a because b^0=1 for b>0.
Initial value: f(0). Growth factor: b>1. Decay factor: 0<b<1. The y-intercept is the point (0,f(0)).
For f(x)=a·b^x, f(0)=a. For a shifted model f(x)=a·b^(x−h)+k, f(0)=a·b^(−h)+k. Never read a alone when the model is shifted.
Equation: replace x with 0. Table or graph: find input zero. Consecutive values: calculate the factor and divide backward until input zero.
P(t)=300(1.04)^t. P(0)=300(1.04)^0=300. Check P(1)=312, showing 4% growth after the start.
M(t)=240(0.75)^t. M(0)=240; the 25% decrease happens each subsequent period.
Enter: y=300(1.04)^x. Look for: the y-intercept (0,300). Use it to answer: initial value is 300. Why it works: b^0=1. Faster or not? Reading a in a·b^x is faster; Desmos is useful to verify visually.
In 300(1.04)^t, 300 is the start, 1.04 is the factor, and 4% is the growth rate. Shifted exponents change f(0). A decay model may have a large initial amount.
If the equation is standard, read a. If shifted, substitute zero. If only a later value is given, divide by b^number of periods.
1) 70(1.2)^t starts at 70. 2) 4·3^(x+1) starts at 12. 3) f(1)=50 with b=2 starts at 25.
Initial value=f(0). Standard model: a. Shifted model: substitute zero. Table/graph: input zero. Later value: divide backward by the factor.
